title: Cap. II open: Variæ sententiæ — election from foresight merits; agenda
latin: CAP. II. Variae illorum sententiae referuntur, qui electionem praevisis nostris meritis inniti docuerunt. Accedamus tandem ad ipsum negotium cui hanc operam nostram destinavimus. Et primo de Electione sive Praedestinatione ad salutem & aeternam beatitudinem disputabimus: dein ad illam alteram hujus controversiae partem, de Non-electione, Praeteritione, sive reprobatione deveniemus.
pass_a: CAP. II. The various opinions of those are rehearsed who have taught that election rests upon our foresight merits. Let us approach at last to the very business to which we have destined this our labor. And first we will dispute concerning Election or Predestination unto salvation and eternal blessedness: thereafter we will come to that other part of this controversy, concerning Non-election, Passing-by, or reprobation. Key lemmas: variae sententiae (various opinions); merita praevisa (foresight merits); electio / praedestinatio; non-electio / praeteritio / reprobatio.
pass_b: CAP. II. Here I set out the various opinions of those who teach that election rests on our foresight merits. We come at last to the business this labor was meant for. First we will argue election — or predestination — to salvation and eternal blessedness; then the other half of the controversy: non-election, passing-by, or reprobation.

title: Cap. II: principal question — foresight act as merit/cause of election?
latin: Principale quaesitum quod attinet ad prius membrum futurae disceptationis, hoc est; Utrum in illis qui eliguntur & praedestinantur ad gloriam, detur aliquis actus aut qualitas a Deo praevisa & praeconsiderata, aut aliud quodcunque, quod sit meritum, causa, ratio, conditio, aut antecedens quolibet modo ita praesuppositum decreto electionis, ut ex positione talis praecedanei in praevisione Divina ponatur electio, ex negatione, negetur. Quid sentiant hac de re Pelagiani, quid Scholastici, quid nuperi quidam Doctores, videamus.
pass_a: The principal question which pertains to the prior member of the coming disputation is this: Whether in those who are elected and predestined unto glory there is given some act or quality foresight and preconsidered by God, or anything whatsoever, which is a merit, cause, reason, condition, or antecedent in any way so presupposed to the decree of election, that from the positing of such a preceding thing in the Divine foresight election is posited, and from its negation it is denied. What the Pelagians sense on this matter, what the Scholastics, what certain recent Doctors, let us see. Key lemmas: quaesitum principale (principal question); actus / qualitas praevisa (foresight act/quality); meritum / causa / conditio; decretum electionis.
pass_b: The chief question for the first half of the coming dispute is this: in those elected and predestined to glory, is there some act or quality God foresaw and weighed beforehand — or anything at all — that stands as merit, cause, reason, condition, or antecedent so bound to the decree of election that when that prior thing is set in the Divine foresight election follows, and when it is denied election is denied? Let us see what Pelagians, Scholastics, and certain recent doctors hold on this.

title: Cap. II: Pelagian opening — free will alone; election from foresight holiness
latin: Dari tale aliquod praecedaneum, cui semper innitatur decretum electionis, humana ratio amore sui occaecata praetendit, Scriptura reclamante. Britannus ille coluber hoc plenum veneni & pestilentiae dogma evomuit, Posse hominem solis viribus liberi sui arbitrii legem Dei servare, ad vitam aeternam pervenire. Huic & illud alterum conjunxit ejusdem virulentiae, Deum scilicet praevidentem quinam essent per voluntatis suae arbitrium sancte victuri, eos omnes ante jacta mundi fundamenta ad gloriam elegisse.
pass_a: That such a preceding thing is given, upon which the decree of election always rests, human reason blinded by love of itself pretends, Scripture crying out against it. That British serpent vomited forth this dogma full of poison and pestilence: That a human is able by the sole powers of his free choice to keep the law of God, to arrive at eternal life. To this he joined that other of the same virulence: namely that God, foresighting who would live holy through the choice of their will, elected all those unto glory before the foundations of the world were laid. Key lemmas: praecedaneum (preceding ground); Britannus coluber (British serpent = Pelagius); liberum arbitrium (free choice); praescientia sanctitatis (foresight of holiness).
pass_b: Blinded self-love in human reason claims there is always some prior ground on which the decree of election rests — and Scripture cries against it. That British serpent spat out this poison: that a person can keep God's law and reach eternal life by free choice alone. He joined to it another venom of the same kind: that God, foresighting who would live holy by their own will's choice, elected them all to glory before the world's foundations were laid.

title: Cap. II: Augustine vs Pelagius; dogma already rejected — no fresh refutation
latin: Utrumque colligitur ex Augustino: prius ex Epist. 89. Ubi Anathema vibrat contra Pelagianos ob haeresin praedictam, Illud quod dicunt, sufficere homini liberum arbitrium ad dominica praecepta implenda, omnino anathematizandum est, & omnibus exsecrationibus detestandum. Posterius ex De praedestin. Sanctor. lib. 1. cap. 18. Praesciebat ergo, ait Pelagianus, qui futuri erant sancti per liberae voluntatis arbitrium, & ideo eos ante mundi constitutionem in ipsa sua praescientia, qua tales futuros esse praescivit, elegit. Sed quia Pelagium atque Pelagianum hoc dogma omnes omnium sectarum Theologi jam rejiciunt, aut saltem videri volunt rejecisse, non facessam mihi negotii in illis refellendis, quae nemo audet aperte propugnare.
pass_a: Both are gathered from Augustine: the former from Epistle 89, where he brandishes an Anathema against the Pelagians on account of the aforesaid heresy: That which they say, that free choice suffices for a human to fulfill the Lord's precepts, is altogether to be anathematized, and to be detested with all execrations. The latter from On the Predestination of the Saints, book 1, chapter 18: God foresaw, says the Pelagian, who would be holy through the choice of free will, and therefore before the constitution of the world he elected them in that very foresight of his by which he foresaw them to be such. But because all theologians of every sect already reject Pelagius and this Pelagian dogma, or at least wish to seem to have rejected it, I will not make business for myself in refuting those things which no one dares openly to defend. Key lemmas: anathema; Epist. 89; De praedestinatione sanctorum; dogma Pelagianum.
pass_b: Augustine supplies both. First, Epistle 89, where he hurls anathema at the Pelagians for that heresy: their claim that free choice alone is enough to keep the Lord's commands is to be anathematized and cursed outright. Second, On the Predestination of the Saints 1.18: God foresaw, says the Pelagian, who would be holy by free will's choice, and so before the world's founding he elected them in that very foresight by which he foresaw them to be such. But since theologians of every party already reject Pelagius and this Pelagian dogma — or at least want to look as if they have — I will not waste effort refuting what no one dares openly defend.

lemmas.gloss: On the Predestination of the Saints

title: Cap. II: Semipelagians — initiative from us; perseverance by free will
latin: Pelagii venenatum dogma Semipelagiani ex parte amplexi sunt; in queis numero Faustum Regiensem, Cassianum Collatorem, Massilienses, aliosque omnes, qui confitentes gratiae necessitatem ad pie vivendum, in pietate perseverandum, & vitam aeternam consequendam, defendunt tamen ex nobis praecedere quoddam initium laboris & conatus, quod Divina gratia subsequitur, & cujus intuitu haec gratia salutaris nobis donatur. Tenent etiam consequenter, postquam homo conando & laborando Dei gratiam adeptus est, non per donum aliquod quod manat ab electione, sed per liberum arbitrium suum perseverare in hac gratia, fide, & bonis operibus; atque ex praescientia talis voluntatis eligi ad vitam aeternam.
pass_a: The Semipelagians have embraced Pelagius's poisoned dogma in part; in which number are Faustus of Riez, Cassian the Conferencer, the Massilians, and all others who, confessing the necessity of grace for living piously, persevering in piety, and obtaining eternal life, nevertheless defend that from us there precedes a certain beginning of labor and striving, which Divine grace follows, and in view of which this saving grace is given to us. They also hold consequently that after a human by striving and laboring has obtained God's grace, he perseveres in this grace, faith, and good works not through some gift that flows from election, but through his free choice; and that from the foresight of such a will he is elected unto eternal life. Key lemmas: Semipelagiani; initium laboris & conatus (beginning of labor and striving); Faustus Regiensis; Cassianus; Massilienses; praescientia voluntatis.
pass_b: The Semipelagians took up part of Pelagius's poison. Count among them Faustus of Riez, Cassian the Conferencer, the Massilians, and all who admit grace is needed to live godly, persevere, and reach eternal life — yet still claim that from us there first comes a beginning of labor and effort, which God's grace then follows, and for the sake of which saving grace is given. Consequently they hold that once a person has gained God's grace by striving and labor, he stays in that grace, faith, and good works not by any gift flowing from election, but by his own free choice; and that election to eternal life rests on foresight of that will.

title: Cap. II: Faustus — initiative, progress, election from foresight merits
latin: De praevio conatu & labore scribit Faustus lib. 1. cap. 12. Sicut sui criminis est, quod filius prodigus longe pii parentis fugit oculos, ita suae est devotionis, quod per insitum sibi bonum deliberans & assurgens, ad paternos recurrit amplexus. Et cap. 17. Dominus invitat volentem, attrahit desiderantem, erigit adnitentem. Et cap. ult. Voluntatem ejus qui est purgandus, exspectat. De progressu & perseverantia per vires liberi arbitrii, non per donum aliquod speciale manans a decreto praedestinationis, sic philosophatur, Lib. 2. sect. 5. Salutem hominis non in praedestinatione Factoris, sed in operatione famulantis largitor gratiae collocavit. Et Cap. 12. Status hominis in diversa, non pro constitutione Dei, sed pro arbitrii libertate potest versari. Denique electionem nostram ex praescientia hujusmodi bonae voluntatis & operationis nostrae, non ex Dei decreto aliquo antecedente, aperte docet lib. 2. sect. 2. Praescientia Dei de materia humanorum actuum sumit exordium. Et paulo post, Aliud est praescire, aliud praedestinare. Praescientia gerenda praenoscit, postmodum praedestinatio retribuenda describit. Illa praevidet merita, haec praeordinat praemia. Praescientia ad potentiam, praedestinatio ad justitiam pertinet. Nisi praescientia exploraverit, praedestinatio nihil decernit. Hisce verbis non a gratia praedestinationis arcessit merita, sed a praevisis meritis praedestinationem.
pass_a: Concerning the prior striving and labor Faustus writes in book 1, chapter 12: Just as it is of his own crime that the prodigal son fled far from the eyes of a pious parent, so it is of his own devotion that, deliberating and rising through the good implanted in him, he runs back to the paternal embraces. And chapter 17: The Lord invites the willing, draws the desiring, raises the striving. And the last chapter: He waits for the will of him who is to be purged. Concerning progress and perseverance through the powers of free choice, not through some special gift flowing from the decree of predestination, he philosophizes thus, book 2, section 5: He has placed the salvation of a human not in the Maker's predestination, but in the operation of the one serving the Giver of grace. And chapter 12: A human's state can turn in diverse ways not according to God's constitution, but according to the liberty of choice. Finally he openly teaches our election from the foresight of such a good will and operation of ours, not from some antecedent decree of God, book 2, section 2: God's foresight takes its beginning from the matter of human acts. And a little after: It is one thing to foresee, another to predestine. Foresight knows beforehand what is to be done; afterward predestination describes what is to be repaid. That foresights merits; this preordains rewards. Foresight pertains to power, predestination to justice. Unless foresight has explored, predestination decrees nothing. By these words he does not fetch merits from the grace of predestination, but predestination from foresight merits. Key lemmas: Faustus; conatus praevius; praescientia / praedestinatio; merita praevisa.
pass_b: On that prior effort and labor Faustus writes (1.12): just as the prodigal's flight from a pious father's eyes is his own crime, so his return to the father's embrace — deliberating and rising by the good planted in him — is his own devotion. Chapter 17: the Lord invites the willing, draws the desiring, raises the striving. The last chapter: he waits for the will of the one to be cleansed. On progress and perseverance by free choice's powers — not by any special gift flowing from the predestination decree — he reasons (2.5): human salvation is set not in the Maker's predestination, but in the working of the one who serves the Giver of grace. Chapter 12: a person's state can turn this way or that not by God's constitution, but by liberty of choice. At last he openly teaches election from foresight of such good will and working of ours, not from any prior decree of God (2.2): God's foresight begins from the matter of human acts. A little later: to foresee is one thing, to predestine another. Foresight knows beforehand what is to be done; then predestination marks out what is to be repaid. That foresights merits; this preordains rewards. Foresight belongs to power, predestination to justice. Unless foresight has searched, predestination decides nothing. In these words he does not draw merits from the grace of predestination — he draws predestination from foresight merits.

title: Cap. II: Prosper & Hilary on Massilians — Semipelagian close before Scholastics
latin: Sed horum Semipelagianorum sententia clarissime intelligi potest ex Epistola Prosperi & Hilarii ad Augustinum, quae ambae praefiguntur libro quem inscripsit Augustinus De praedestinatione sanctorum. De istis sic scribit Prosper, Haec ipsorum definitio est; Qui credituri sunt, quive in ea fide, quae deinceps per Dei gratiam sit juvanda, mansuri sunt, praescisse ante mundi constitutionem Deum, & eos praedestinasse in regnum suum, quos gratis vocatos, dignos futuros electione, & de hac vita bono fine excessuros praeviderit. Et Hilarius, Massilienses inutile esse praedicationi dicant, quod quidam secundum propositum eligendi dicantur, &c. Et pauculis interjectis, Asserunt eo merito, quo voluerit & crediderit unusquisque, a suo morbo se posse sanari, & ipsius fidei augmentum, & totius sanctitatis suae consequi effectum. De compendio, putant rationem reddi electorum vel rejectorum in eo, quod unicuique meritum propriae voluntatis adjungitur. Concedunt Deum non eligere opera cujusquam in praescientia quae ipse donaturus est; sed affirmant, fidem eligere in praescientia, ut quem crediturum esse praescivit, ipsum elegerit, cui spiritum sanctum donet, ut bene operando aeternam vitam consequeretur. Denique, nemini dari talem perseverantiam putant, a qua non permittitur praevaricari; atque idcirco non admittunt eligendorum & rejiciendorum esse numerum definitum. Haec paulo latius recitanda putavi, ut videatis, quam prope absint a Pelagianis aut Semipelagianis, qui nostro hoc saeculo Augustini doctrinam, in sacris Scripturis fundatam, & catholicae Ecclesiae testimonio olim confirmatam, explosum eunt.
pass_a: But the opinion of these Semipelagians can most clearly be understood from the Letter of Prosper and of Hilary to Augustine, both of which are prefixed to the book which Augustine titled On the Predestination of the Saints. Concerning these Prosper writes thus: This is their definition; That God foresaw before the constitution of the world who would believe, or who would remain in that faith which afterward is to be helped by God's grace, and that he predestined unto his kingdom those whom, called by grace, he foresaw would be worthy of election, and would depart from this life with a good end. And Hilary: The Massilians say it is useless for preaching that certain ones are said to be elect according to purpose, &c. And with a few words interposed: They assert that by that merit by which each one has willed and believed, he can be healed from his disease, and obtain the increase of that very faith and the effect of his whole holiness. In short, they think the reason of the elect or rejected is rendered in this, that to each one the merit of his own will is joined. They grant that God does not elect anyone's works in foresight which he himself is going to give; but they affirm that he elects faith in foresight, so that whom he foresaw would believe, him he elected, to whom he might give the Holy Spirit, that by working well he might obtain eternal life. Finally, they think such perseverance is given to no one from which he is not permitted to fall away; and therefore they do not admit that there is a definite number of those to be elected and rejected. I thought these things should be recited a little more fully, that you may see how near they are to the Pelagians or Semipelagians who in this our age go about to explode Augustine's doctrine, founded in the sacred Scriptures and formerly confirmed by the testimony of the catholic Church. Key lemmas: Prosper; Hilarius; Massilienses; meritum propriae voluntatis; numerus electorum definitus.
pass_b: These Semipelagians are clearest in the letters of Prosper and Hilary to Augustine — both prefixed to Augustine's On the Predestination of the Saints. Prosper reports their definition: God foresaw before the world's founding who would believe, or who would stay in the faith later helped by his grace, and predestined to his kingdom those he foresaw, once called by grace, would be worthy of election and would leave this life with a good end. Hilary: the Massilians say it empties preaching to speak of some as elect according to purpose, and so on. A few lines later: they claim that by the merit of each person's willing and believing, one can be healed of disease and gain both the increase of that faith and the full effect of one's holiness. In short, they put the reason for elect or reject in this: each is paired with the merit of his own will. They grant God does not elect anyone's works in foresight of gifts he himself will give; yet they affirm he elects faith in foresight — so that whom he foresaw would believe, he elected, and to him gives the Holy Spirit so that by good works he may reach eternal life. Finally they hold that no one is given such perseverance that falling away is impossible; and so they deny any fixed number of those to be elected and rejected. I thought this worth quoting a little more fully, so you may see how near they stand to the Pelagians or Semipelagians who in our own age try to explode Augustine's teaching — rooted in Scripture and long confirmed by the catholic Church's witness.
